articles.title: Weather on the board today
articles.body:
A dense overcast of engineering recruitment anxiety settled over the board early, dominated by the GATE versus JEE debate. Anon claimed the GATE syllabus was cognitively lighter, confessing to passing boards on luck alone despite zero study.

The pressure system was heavy, with forty-six distinct posts confirming the frustration of the curriculum gap. By midday, a cold front of religious historiography hit.

One Anon asserted Hinduism was a twentieth-century invention, triggering a squall of counter-arguments from the Itihasa camp. Those respondents insisted the Ramayana and Mahabharata constituted actual history, creating a turbulent zone of memory disputes that lasted through the afternoon.

The evening brought a scattered drizzle of near-death stories and geopolitical sniping. Anons swapped tales of surviving violence while simultaneously attacking the Sikh protagonist of the film Dhurandhar.

One poster called the hero a slur-laden term, linking the casting choice to R&AW operations in Canada. The storm subsided as the night fog rolled in, leaving the board damp and silent.

articles.title: GATE vs JEE and the RAM Manufacturing Debate
articles.body:
Anon asked whether the GATE syllabus is relative cognitively easier than the JEE syllabus, noting that they did not remember studying for board exams but found GATE preparation straightforward compared to PCM.

Another Anon replied that India should really manufacture RAM and SSDs, stating the market is too brutal for these two components. This comment shifted the thread’s focus from exam difficulty to semiconductor production.

A third Anon responded to the manufacturing point, noting that the first semiconductor investment in India was a Micron ATMP plan for 2.75 billion dollars, which produces memory devices.

A fourth Anon added that CXMT is manufacturing more RAM, but the quality is bad as of now. The thread moved from personal academic difficulty to the state of Indian semiconductor infrastructure, specifically memory chips.

The initial question about GATE and JEE difficulty was answered indirectly by the shift in conversation. The mention of Micron’s investment and CXMT’s output anchored the discussion in specific industrial facts rather than general complaints.

Anon did not return to the original question of whether GATE is easier than JEE, but the thread’s trajectory showed a clear pivot.

The cognitive ease of GATE became a minor point in a larger discussion about why India lacks domestic RAM and SSD production.

The brutal market for memory components was cited as a reason for the lack of local manufacturing, while the existence of foreign investments and Chinese exports provided context.

The thread ended without a definitive answer on exam difficulty, but with a concrete picture of the semiconductor landscape. Anon’s initial confusion over GATE was resolved by the fact that the topic changed entirely.

articles.title: OP Claims Hinduism Is a Modern Invention
articles.body:
Anon posted the bare statement that Hinduism was invented in the twentieth century. The remark stood alone, devoid of citation or elaboration, inviting immediate scrutiny from the rest of the board.

A respondent called for the OP to bring the claim to Tamil Nadu, noting the presence of five-thousand-year-old temples in the region.

The reply served as a direct physical counterpoint to the chronological argument, grounding the dispute in specific architectural heritage rather than abstract historical narratives. Another user replied in Romanized Urdu, stating that the fire had been lit by a Hyderabadi Pasmande.

The comment shifted the frame from theological history to ethnic and regional mockery, targeting the OP’s perceived origin or political alignment rather than addressing the factual claim about the religion’s antiquity.

A third respondent responded with a profane Hindi insult, telling the OP to mind his own harlot. This interaction demonstrated the thread’s rapid descent from a pseudo-historical assertion into a standard exchange of slurs.

The OP did not return to the thread after the initial post, leaving the claim unchallenged by its author but dismissed by the responders through either geographical evidence or personal abuse.

The thread illustrates the board’s tendency to treat broad civilizational claims as bait for identity-based harassment. Rather than engaging with the academic debate over the term Hinduism or the dating of Vedic texts, the users focused on regional pride and sectarian insults.

The five-thousand-year temple remark was the only substantive counter-argument, while the other two replies reduced the discourse to ethnic taunts and vulgarities.

articles.title: Itihasa, Homer, and the Problem of Memory
articles.body:
Anon asserted that the Ramayana and Mahabharata constitute Itihasa, a term translating to history. The immediate response was a mix of skepticism, archaeological citation, and tribal dismissal.

One Anon replied that the texts are merely the Indian equivalent of the Iliad and Odyssey, noting the complete lack of archeological evidence for the events described.

Another respondent countered with specific data, pointing to the BORI critical edition and arguing that Pānini’s Ashtadhyayi from the 6th century BC explicitly references the Mahabharata war, Vāsudev, and Arjuna.

This respondent further cited 2nd century CE Vrishni coins depicting Krishna as material proof of the figures' existence. The conversation quickly shifted from textual analysis to broader theories of historiography.

One Anon argued that if a story is passed down through generations by victors, it retains some core truth.

Applying this logic, this Anon claimed Muhammad was likely a real person, though the miraculous events attributed to him were the "schizo shit" of a successful warlord.

Another Anon offered a similar assessment for the Hindu epics, suggesting Rama and Krishna were probably real kings whose stories were heavily altered over time.

A different Anon proposed that the Pushpak vimana was not a flying machine but a metaphor for a chariot or ship, a technology that was lost to history long before the Wright brothers. Frustration with the debate manifested in several directions.

One Anon dismissed the skeptics as low IQ individuals who took metaphors too literally. Another accused Brahmins of creating the gods and idols as tools to keep the population in check.

The thread also featured a sharp exchange regarding media adaptations, with one Anon sarcastically noting that the only high-quality media based on this history had to be made by Japanese creators.

The final note in the sequence was a methodological warning: the farther one travels back in time, the harder it becomes to separate legend from fact due to the loss of documentation.

The thread ended without resolving whether these texts are history or high-fantasy literature.

articles.title: Anonymous Users Share Near-Death Experiences
articles.body:
Anons shared stories of killing or nearly killing others. One anon, ten years old, kicked his six-year-old brother in the chest over a remote control. The boy fainted, his face turning red, until the older brother performed CPR and revived him.

Another anon described pouring Harpic into his sister's food. His mother smelled the dish, found it odd, and threw it away, preventing any harm.

A third anon, identifying as an intern doctor, claimed to have killed a Tamil baby in a government hospital, stating he felt like the god Ram. Responses mixed dark humor with confusion.

One poster asked how the victim's parents reacted, while another simply called the doctor a NEET. The thread also included unrelated jokes about cello tape on genitals and accusations of being a torbottom.

articles.title: Anon Criticizes Dhurandhar's Sikh Protagonist Amid R&AW Debates
articles.body:
Anon declared the film Dhurandhar inferior, labeling its Sikh protagonist a cuck and accusing director Aditya Dhar of ignoring the irony that R&AW operations in Canada target Sikhs.

The thread quickly devolved into arguments about the ethnic composition of intelligence officers. One anon suggested a South Indian Hindu would have been more realistic, while another countered that Sikhs are high-testosterone men, making the casting logical.

Replies mixed racial slurs with complaints about the film's music, which one viewer described as ear-raping rap.

The group debated whether the actor’s appearance fitted a Pakistani masquerade, with some mocking his height and others claiming he would look South Asian regardless. The final posts returned to personal insults directed at the director.
